blocks.text: An encoder model reads an entire input sequence at once and produces a rich representation of it, one that captures the meaning of every token in light of every other token in that same sequence, both before and after it.

This bidirectional view is the defining feature of encoder models, and it shapes exactly what they are good at, understanding and classifying text, and what they are not built for, generating new text one word at a time.
1. What an Encoder Model Actually Does

blocks.alt: What an Encoder Model Actually Does
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216681-942983558.png

Given an input sequence, an encoder model produces a set of vectors, one per token, where each vector encodes that token meaning as shaped by the full surrounding sentence, not just the words that came before it.
These vectors are useful directly as embeddings, or as the input to a smaller task specific layer added on top for classification, extraction, or similarity comparisons.
2. Bidirectional Context, The Defining Trait
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216682-623615808.png
When an encoder processes a sentence, every token attends to every other token in that sentence, the words before it and the words after it, all at once, in a single pass.

This is different from a model that only sees what came before a given position, and it is exactly why encoder models tend to produce strong representations for understanding tasks, since full context is available immediately rather than accumulated one step at a time.
3. A Concrete Architecture Example, BERT
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216683-548312054.png

BERT, short for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, is the model that popularized this architecture, stacking many encoder layers on top of each other, each one refining the token representations produced by the layer before it.
Many later encoder models, used widely for search and classification tasks today, follow the same basic shape BERT established, even when their training data or size differs considerably.
4. Masked Language Modeling as the Training Objective

blocks.alt: Masked Language Modeling as the Training Objective
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216683-705952484.png

Encoder models are typically pretrained using masked language modeling, a portion of the input tokens are hidden, replaced with a special mask token, and the model is trained to predict what word was actually there, using the surrounding context on both sides.
This objective forces the model to build genuinely bidirectional understanding, since predicting a masked word in the middle of a sentence requires using both the words before and after it.

blocks.title: A different objective than decoder models
blocks.content: This masked prediction objective is distinct from the next token prediction objective used to pretrain decoder models, a difference covered directly in the next topic.

blocks.text: 5. What Encoder Models Are Good At

blocks.alt: What Encoder Models Are Good At
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216684-638813806.png

Because encoder models produce strong, context aware representations rather than generating new text, they excel at tasks like sentiment classification, named entity recognition, semantic search, and producing embeddings for retrieval systems.

blocks.text: 6. What Encoder Models Are Not Built For

blocks.alt: What Encoder Models Are Not Built For
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216684-882305260.png

Encoder models are not naturally suited to generating open-ended text, writing an essay, answering a question in full sentences, or holding a conversation, since their bidirectional design assumes the full input is already available, which does not fit generating text one new word at a time.
This is the main reason modern conversational assistants are built on decoder models rather than encoder models, a contrast the next topic covers directly.
7. Encoder Output, Embeddings Rather Than Generated Text

The direct output of an encoder model is a set of numeric vectors, not readable text. Turning that output into something usable requires either comparing those vectors mathematically, as in search and clustering, or feeding them into a small additional layer trained for a specific task, as in classification.

# A simplified encoder classification pattern
embeddings = encoder_model(input_text)
logits = classification_head(embeddings)
predicted_label = argmax(logits)

blocks.text: 8. Fine-Tuning an Encoder Model for Classification

blocks.alt: Fine-Tuning an Encoder Model for Classification
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216684-310661084.png

Fine-tuning an encoder model for a specific classification task typically means adding a small new layer on top of the pretrained encoder, then training that combination on labeled examples for the target task, spam detection, topic labeling, or sentiment analysis, for instance.

This kind of fine-tuning is usually fast and requires comparatively little data, since the encoder already brings strong general language understanding, and only the small added layer, plus some adjustment to the encoder itself, needs to specialize.
9. Encoder Models in the Fine-Tuning Landscape Today

While decoder based large language models dominate headlines, encoder models remain the workhorse behind search systems, content moderation pipelines, and many classification tasks where the goal is understanding rather than generating text.

Choosing an encoder model instead of a much larger decoder model for a pure classification task often means a smaller, faster, cheaper fine-tuned system, without sacrificing accuracy on that specific job.
Worked Example

A team building a content moderation system needs to classify incoming posts into safe, needs review, or unsafe. They fine-tune a pretrained encoder model by adding a three way classification head on top and training on fifteen thousand labeled posts.

The resulting model runs quickly, since it is far smaller than a general purpose decoder based language model, and reaches strong accuracy on this narrow classification task, because the bidirectional encoder representation is well suited to understanding a post in full context before making a single decision.
Common Mistakes

items: Trying to use an encoder model for open-ended text generation, a task its architecture is not built for
Forgetting to add and train a task specific head when fine-tuning an encoder for classification
Choosing a large decoder based model for a pure classification task where a smaller encoder model would work just as well, faster and cheaper
Assuming masked language modeling and next token prediction are the same training objective

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a classification task you are familiar with, spam detection or topic labeling, for example, and sketch what an encoder based fine-tuning setup would look like, the input, the added classification head, and the kind of labeled data you would need.
Key Takeaway

Encoder models read an entire input at once and build bidirectional, context aware representations well suited to classification, search, and extraction tasks, but they are not designed for generating new open-ended text, which is the role decoder models fill instead.
